paper_a.title: Phase transition of the largest eigenvalue for non-null complex sample covariance matrices

paper_b.title: On the Distribution of the Length of the Longest Increasing Subsequence of Random Permutations

metadata.description: Both papers prove Tracy-Widom-type limits for largest-eigenvalue / largest-row-length statistics via Riemann-Hilbert / Fredholm-determinant steepest-descent. Baik-Deift-Johansson (paper B, 1999) establishes the Tracy-Widom $F_{GUE}$ limit for the longest increasing subsequence of a random permutation, anchoring the universality class. BBP (paper A, 2005) extends Tracy-Widom universality to the spiked complex sample-covariance model: it preserves $F_0=F_{GUE}$ in the sub-critical regime and discovers a new family of limit distributions $F_k$ (Airy + finite-rank perturbation) and a Gaussian regime $G_k$ governed by the spike strength. The relation is a clean extension: the same machinery (Fredholm determinant, Airy/PII parametrix, steep-descent contour) now produces a phase transition rather than a single universal law.

matches.explanation: BBP's primary random object is the sample covariance matrix $S=\frac1N XX^*$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\cdots$; BDJ's primary object is the longest increasing subsequence length $l_N$ of a uniform random permutation. Both papers single out the largest of an integer-indexed family of sample statistics whose distribution is the focus of the paper. They are conceptually parallel as 'the random observable whose Tracy-Widom limit we will prove' but the underlying objects differ (eigenvalue of a Wishart-type matrix vs combinatorial statistic on $S_N$).

BBP's Airy kernel $\mathbf{A}(u,v)=(Ai(u)Ai'(v)-Ai'(u)Ai(v))/(u-v)$ is the central operator from which all limiting distributions are built. BDJ never directly defines the Airy kernel as a node; the Airy function appears only inside the Hastings-McLeod boundary condition for PII (DP328.3). The Airy-kernel formulation is a BBP contribution at this granularity.

BBP's $F_k(x)=\det(1-\mathbf{A}_x)\cdot\det(\delta_{mn}-\langle(1-\mathbf{A}_x)^{-1}s^{(m)},t^{(n)}\rangle)$ specializes at $k=0$ to $F_{GUE}(x)=\det(1-\mathbf{A}_x)$, which is precisely BDJ's Tracy-Widom $F(t)=\exp(-\int_t^\infty(x-t)u^2(x)\,dx)$ via the Tracy-Widom Painlevé-II identity. BBP defines a one-parameter family extending this distribution; BDJ uses the canonical $F_0$. Analogous because the BBP definition strictly generalizes the BDJ object.

BBP's finite GUE distribution $G_k(x)$ is the law of the largest eigenvalue of a $k\times k$ GUE matrix and governs the super-critical regime of the spiked model. BDJ has no finite-$N$ Gaussian-regime analogue; this is a BBP-specific contribution arising from spike-induced phase transition.

Interpolating distributions $F_k(x;w_1,\dots,w_k)$ describe BBP's critical-window scaling between sub-critical and super-critical regimes. No counterpart in BDJ, which has a single universal limit and no spike parameter.

BBP's last-passage-percolation random variable $L(N,M)=\max_\pi\sum X(i,j)$ is used in section 6 to give a heuristic for the critical value. BDJ also has a deep LPP/RSK connection (visible in RP328.1 and the Coulomb-gas remark RP328.2), but at the node level BDJ does not define an LPP variable: the link to RSK is through the Robinson-Schensted bijection on permutations, which gives $l_N$ as the first row of a Young tableau. Same circle of ideas, but no node-level definitional match.

Both papers cite the same Tracy-Widom (1994) GUE largest-eigenvalue theorem as external prior: paper A as TP327.1 (Tracy-Widom GUE limit, attributed to Forrester / Johansson for sample-covariance variant) and paper B as TP328.4 (Tracy-Widom 1994). The cited result is the same, justifying an exact-but-external match. Per the prompt rules this match is informational only and does not contribute to the pair's relation type.
Péché's earlier sub-critical result (TP327.2) is cited prior work specific to spiked covariance. BDJ has no spiked-model precursor.

These are the main theorems of the two papers. BDJ's Theorem 1.1: $\chi_N=(l_N-2\sqrt N)/N^{1/6}\Rightarrow F$ (Tracy-Widom $F_0$). BBP's Theorem 1.4: scaled $\lambda_1$ converges to $F_k$ (sub-critical / critical) or $G_k$ (super-critical), with a phase transition at $\ell_1=1+\gamma^{-1}$. Both are limit theorems for the largest of a family of sample statistics; BBP extends BDJ's universality by introducing a spike parameter and discovering new limit families. The match is analogous because BDJ proves a single universal law whereas BBP proves a regime-dependent phase transition; at $k=0$ the sub-critical BBP limit reduces to the BDJ Tracy-Widom limit.
BBP's interpolating-regime theorem (Theorem 1.6) parametrizes the critical-window scaling of distinguished population eigenvalues. No BDJ analogue.

Convergence in probability of $\lambda_1$ in the two regimes is a corollary specific to the spiked model. BDJ proves $l_N/\sqrt N\to 2$ (Ulam's constant), but this appears only as the centering inside Theorem 1.1, not as a separate corollary node.
Finite-dimensional ($N=k$ fixed) Gaussian limit of $\lambda_1$ is BBP-specific; arises from the super-critical regime structure.
Real-sample analogue conjecture is about extending BBP to real Wishart matrices (GOE-symmetry class). No BDJ analogue.

BBP's Proposition 2.1 expresses $\mathbb{P}(\lambda_1\le\xi)=\det(1-\mathbf{K}_{M,N}|_{(\xi,\infty)})$ as a Fredholm determinant of a kernel built from a double contour integral. BDJ's analogue is the Toeplitz determinant representation $\phi_n(\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}D_{n-1}$ (DP328.6) plus orthonormal polynomials on the unit circle (DP328.7). Both convert the original probability into a determinantal point-process / orthogonal-polynomial expression suitable for steep-descent. The form of the determinant differs (continuous Fredholm vs discrete Toeplitz) because the underlying ensembles differ, but the conceptual role is identical.

BBP Propositions 3.1 and 4.1 give Hilbert-Schmidt convergence of the rescaled kernels $\mathcal{H},\mathcal{J}$ to Airy / Gaussian limits in the sub- and super-critical regimes respectively. BDJ Lemmas 5.1 and 6.4 give regime-by-regime asymptotics of $\kappa_{q-1}^2(\lambda)$ for $\gamma\le 1$ and $\gamma>1$ respectively, including a double-scaling Painlevé-II regime. Both decompose the parameter range into $\gamma<\gamma_c$ / $\gamma=\gamma_c$ / $\gamma>\gamma_c$ and use steep-descent on the orthogonal-polynomial / kernel data. Cluster correspondence; the BBP propositions are kernel-level whereas the BDJ lemmas are scalar-level (norm $\kappa^2$), but they play the same analytic role in producing the limit distribution.

Steep-descent analytic lemmas. BBP LP327.1/2 (Airy regime) and LP327.4/5 (Gaussian regime) verify that the chosen contours $\Gamma,\Sigma$ are steep-descent for the phase function $\pm f$. BDJ LP328.4 (properties of $\alpha(z)$) and LP328.5 (explicit RHP solution $m^\infty$) play the analogous role of providing the phase / equilibrium-measure ingredients on the gap regime $\gamma>1$. Both sets are technical lemmas establishing the contour geometry that drives the asymptotics. The match is analogous because the specific computations (polynomial bounds on $T_1,T_2$ vs explicit formulas for $\alpha, m^\infty$) differ substantially.
Well-definedness of $F_k$ and the polynomial-plus-Airy-integral closed form for $s^{(m)}$ is bookkeeping for BBP's new limit distributions. No counterpart in BDJ.

The Wishart eigenvalue density via Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber is the entry point for BBP's Fredholm formula. BDJ's analogous starting point is Gessel's identity (TP328.3) plus orthogonal polynomials (DP328.7), already paired above. Treating EP327.1 as paper-specific keeps the alignment crisp.

The factorization $\mathbf{K}_{M,N}=\int\mathbf{H}\,\mathbf{J}$ as a Hilbert-Schmidt product is BBP's specific kernel-decomposition strategy. BDJ instead works through the orthogonal-polynomial / RHP representation of $\kappa_q^2$; no direct equation-level analogue.

BBP Proposition 6.1 (last-passage time = largest eigenvalue distributional identity for exponential weights) is part of the LPP coda of paper A. BDJ's analogue would be the RSK / Young-tableau angle (RP328.1, RP328.2) but those are remarks, not nodes claiming a distributional identity, so no match emitted.

Both proofs establish a kernel / RHP representation of the determinant of interest. BBP PP327.1 derives the Fredholm formula via Andreief, Cramer, Hankel contour integrals. BDJ PP328.1 establishes existence/uniqueness of the orthogonal-polynomial RHP $Y$. Different concrete identities (Andreief + HCIZ vs Cauchy-operator + Liouville) but both are the foundational 'represent the probability as a determinant' lemma the rest of the paper rests on.

Sub-critical / Airy-regime convergence. BBP PP327.4 splits $\Gamma=\Gamma'\cup\Gamma''$, applies Lemma 3.1 for the far part, and uses cubic Taylor expansion for the local Airy contribution. BDJ PP328.8 (proof of Lemma 5.1 cases ii, iii) deforms onto $\Sigma^{(3)}$, bounds $\|w^{(3)}\|_\infty,\|w^{(3)}\|_{L^1}$, and introduces a Painlevé-II parametrix near $z=-1$ with $\lambda(z)=q^{1/3}u/(i 2^{4/3})$. Same DKMVZ-style steep-descent, same Painlevé-II / Airy parametrix, same cubic-window scaling $q^{-1/3}$ corresponding to $M^{-1/3}$ in BBP.

Both proofs assemble the limit theorem from the kernel/orthogonal-polynomial asymptotic. BBP PP327.5 proves Theorem 1.4(a): Proposition 3.1 + Airy integral algebra + finite-rank perturbation determinant identity yields $F_k(x)$. BDJ PP328.6 proves Theorem 1.1: Lemma 8.2 sandwich + Lemma 7.1(iii) + integration-by-parts $\frac{d}{dx}2i m^{PII}_{1,22}=u^2$ yields $F(t)$. Both pipelines have the same shape: convert the asymptotic of the analytic ingredient into the limit of the probability via an explicit identity for the limiting distribution.

Super-critical / Gaussian-regime convergence. BBP PP327.10 uses Cauchy residue at $z=\pi_1$ plus Lemma 4.2 and Gaussian Taylor expansion at scale $a/(\nu\sqrt M)$. BDJ PP328.9 (proof of Lemma 6.4) uses DKMVZ analysis for $\gamma>1$, with a $1/\sqrt q$ scale and a PII parametrix near the critical-window sub-case. Both produce a Gaussian-scale ($\sqrt{\cdot}$) regime distinct from the Airy ($M^{1/3}$ / $q^{1/3}$) regime, with the same residue / parametrix toolkit.

Identification of the Gaussian-regime limit kernel as the $k\times k$ GUE Christoffel-Darboux kernel via Hermite ODE / Rodrigues. This finite-GUE identification is BBP-specific because BDJ has no Gaussian regime.
Direct calculation of the finite-$N$ super-critical case via Selberg normalisation. Specific to BBP.

Proof of Proposition 6.1 via geometric LPP / RSK with $L\to\infty$ limit. BDJ has the Robinson-Schensted angle (RP328.1) but does not produce an analogous geometric-LPP-to-Wishart distributional-identity proof at the node level.

Painlevé II equation $u_{xx}=2u^3+xu$ with Hastings-McLeod boundary condition is the analytic backbone of BDJ's limit identification. BBP develops its limits at the level of the Airy operator $\mathbf{A}_x$ and never invokes PII directly. The two papers thus describe Tracy-Widom in two different (but equivalent) presentations: PII trace integrals (BDJ) vs Airy Fredholm determinants (BBP).

Poissonization $\phi_n(\lambda)=\sum e^{-\lambda}\lambda^N q_{n,N}/N!$ is the de-Poissonization-ready bridge from $S_N$ to a continuous parameter. BBP needs no such device because the sample-covariance setting is already continuous in $N,M$.

Cluster of Riemann-Hilbert problem definitions ($Y$, PII RHPs in three equivalent forms). BBP works directly with double-contour Fredholm-determinant kernels rather than full RHP machinery; the steep-descent contour deformations $\Gamma,\Sigma$ in BBP are conceptually parallel but the input is a kernel, not a $2\times 2$ matrix RHP. Marking these as paper-specific BDJ contributions.

Equilibrium-measure / $g$-function machinery and the spike parameter $\gamma=2\sqrt\lambda/(k+1)$ are central to BDJ's RHP analysis on the unit circle, where the third-order Gross-Witten-Johansson phase transition at $\gamma=1$ structures the proof. BBP has its own steep-descent setup but does not introduce an equilibrium measure or $g$-function; the spike-criticality is parametrized differently (population eigenvalue $\ell_1$ vs $1+\gamma^{-1}$). Conceptually parallel phase transitions but different formal devices.

Centered/scaled $\chi_N=(l_N-2\sqrt N)/N^{1/6}$ is BDJ-specific scaling; the BBP analogue is the $M^{2/3}$ Airy or $\sqrt M$ Gaussian scaling that appears inside Theorem 1.4 statements rather than as a separate definition node.

Convergence of moments for $\chi_N$ (BDJ Theorem 1.2) requires uniform tail bounds via Lemma 7.1. BBP focuses on convergence in distribution and does not state a moment-convergence companion theorem. Paper-specific to BDJ.

Gessel / OPWW Toeplitz-determinant identity is cited external prior work converting permutation counting to Toeplitz determinants. The BBP analogue is the HCIZ-based Wishart eigenvalue density (EP327.1), but that is paper-A original, not external; mismatched origins, no match emitted.
Hastings-McLeod existence/uniqueness for PII (TP328.5) and Szego strong limit theorem (TP328.6) are BDJ-specific cited prior results with no BBP counterpart at the node level.

RHP existence for $Y$, $g$-function properties, and the explicit equilibrium measure for $V=-\frac\gamma2(z+z^{-1})$ are BDJ-specific RHP-machinery lemmas without direct BBP counterparts (BBP uses kernel double-contour formulas, not RHP/$g$-function).
Lower bound on $|e^{-2\alpha}|$ in the gap regime is a technical step inside BDJ's $\gamma>1$ analysis, with no node-level BBP analogue.

BDJ Lemma 7.1 collects the five regime-bounds for $\log\phi_n(\lambda)$. BBP's analogous bookkeeping lives inside Propositions 3.1 and 4.1 (already matched above with cluster LP328.6/LP328.8); LP328.9 is the higher-level aggregation step distinctive to the de-Poissonization pipeline and has no direct BBP node.

De-Poissonization lemmas are needed because BDJ's natural parameter is the Poisson rate $\lambda$ but the theorem is about uniform $S_N$. BBP works directly in $N,M$ and does not need a de-Poissonization step. Paper-specific to BDJ.
Connection of $Y$-RHP to Toda lattice / Painlevé III is integrable-systems context for BDJ. BBP does not claim a Toda / PIII connection.
Tail-bound equation $F_N(t)\le C(M)e^{ct^3}$ etc. is the BDJ ingredient feeding moment convergence (Theorem 1.2). BBP states no analogous tail-bound equation.
Variational characterization of $d\mu_V$ is part of BDJ's equilibrium-measure setup. BBP has no equilibrium-measure node.

The PII trace identity $\frac{d}{dx}2i m^{PII,1}_{1,22}(x)=u^2(x)$ is the bridge from BDJ's RHP residue to the Tracy-Widom $F$ presentation. BBP works in the Airy-determinant presentation throughout and does not need this identity.
Ulam's problem (asymptotics of $\mathbb E(l_N)$) is the historical motivating problem for BDJ. BBP's motivating problem is the spiked-covariance phase transition, which is structurally different.
Variational problem for the equilibrium measure on the unit circle. No BBP counterpart.
